Miguel Tejada, a shortstop for the Houston Astros, has been charged with lying to Congress. The document says Tejada lied to congressional investigators when he told them on August 26, 2005, that he had never heard discussions about steroids by other players, and that he never knew of any other player using steroids. After the December 2007 Mitchell Report on steroid use in baseball, which appeared to contradict Tejada, the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform asked the Justice Department to investigate whether Tejada "made knowingly false statements to the committee." Tejada played for the Athletics from 1997 to 2003. He is scheduled to appear at 11 a.m. Wednesday before a magistrate judge, indicating the charge against him will be a misdemeanor carrying a maximum sentence of a year in jail. However, a government official familiar with the case said that under sentencing guidelines, Tejada could get from zero to 6 months, which means he may receive probation without jail time. # Miguel Tejada Expected to Plead Guilty to Lying to Congress

Miguel Tejada, the veteran shortstop for the Houston Astros, is reportedly set to plead guilty to charges that he lied to Congress regarding his knowledge of performance-enhancing drug use among Major League Baseball players. The plea marks a significant development in the long-running saga surrounding steroid use in professional baseball and represents a legal consequence for one of the sport's prominent players.

## Details of the Allegations

According to a federal court document, Tejada is accused of providing a former teammate with checks totaling more than $5,000 in 2003. Investigators believe these payments were made in connection with the purchase of human growth hormone, a substance banned by MLB due to its performance-enhancing properties. This financial transaction forms a key piece of evidence in the case against him.

## Origins of the Charge

The charge against Tejada traces back to a 2005 interview he gave to congressional investigators, during which he explicitly denied ever hearing about or having knowledge of other players using steroids. At the time, this testimony was accepted as part of the broader congressional effort to understand the scope of drug use in professional baseball.

However, the credibility of Tejada's statements came under scrutiny following the release of the Mitchell Report in December 2007. This comprehensive investigation into steroid use in baseball, conducted by former Senator George Mitchell, contained information that directly contradicted Tejada's earlier denials to Congress. The discrepancies between his sworn testimony and the findings of the report raised serious questions about whether he had been truthful during the congressional inquiry.

## Congressional Response and Investigation

In light of these contradictions, the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform took action by formally requesting that the Justice Department investigate Tejada's 2005 testimony. This request set in motion a federal investigation that has now culminated in the expected guilty plea, demonstrating the seriousness with which Congress treats false statements made during official proceedings.

## Legal Proceedings Ahead

Tejada is scheduled to appear before a federal magistrate judge to formally enter his plea. He faces a misdemeanor charge, which carries a maximum possible sentence of one year in jail. While this represents a relatively lesser charge compared to felony offenses, the case underscores the legal risks players face when providing testimony to congressional committees investigating drug use in professional sports. The outcome of this case may serve as a reminder to other athletes about the seriousness of congressional testimony and the potential consequences of providing false statements to lawmakers.
